questions.q: Why does the basic owner/group/other rwx model run out of road for real-world access control?
options: It only has one owner slot and one group slot, so it can't grant a second specific user or group different access to the same file
It doesn't support the execute bit
It only works on directories, not files
It requires every user to be in the same group
questions.explain: A file has exactly one owner and one group; a second user or group needing different access requires an ACL.

questions.q: What does setfacl -m u:auditor:r-- report.csv actually do?
options: Adds a named ACL entry granting auditor read-only access to report.csv, without changing the file's group
Changes report.csv's owner to auditor
Deletes report.csv
Grants auditor full read/write/execute access
questions.explain: setfacl -m u:user:perms adds or modifies a named-user ACL entry independent of the file's actual group membership.

questions.q: What does a trailing + after the permission string in ls -l output (e.g. -rw-rw-r--+) indicate?
options: The file has an Access Control List beyond the basic owner/group/other permissions
The file is executable
The file is owned by root
The file has the sticky bit set
questions.explain: The + is ls -l's signal that getfacl will show additional named-user or named-group entries.

questions.q: What does the ACL mask entry control?
options: The maximum effective permission any named user or group ACL entry can actually use
Which users are allowed to run setfacl
The file's basic owner permission only
Whether the ACL is readable by getfacl
questions.explain: Even if a named entry grants more, the mask caps what's actually effective, and setfacl recalculates it by default.

questions.q: Why is the sticky bit set on /tmp, and what does it actually prevent?
options: /tmp is world-writable so everyone can create temp files; the sticky bit prevents users from deleting or renaming files they don't own, even though they can write to the directory
It prevents any user from creating new files in /tmp
It encrypts every file created inside /tmp
It makes /tmp read-only for all users except root
questions.explain: Without the sticky bit, write access to a shared directory would let any user delete or rename anyone else's files inside it.
